diabetic-neuropathy.name: Diabetic neuropathy
diabetic-neuropathy.scope: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, mononeuropathy, foot ulcer prevention, pharmacotherapy (duloxetine, pregabalin, TCAs)
diabetic-neuropathy.core: Diabetes damages sensory, motor, and autonomic nerves; identify the pattern, exclude additional causes, relieve pain, and protect insensate feet.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long diabetes duration, chronic hyperglycemia, smoking, kidney disease, dyslipidemia
Alcohol excess and metformin-associated B12 deficiency may coexist and worsen symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Acute asymmetric weakness, marked motor loss**, or rapid progression → investigate another cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Metabolic and microvascular injury damages peripheral axons; longest nerves affected first
Loss of protective sensation plus deformity/ischemia → repetitive unnoticed trauma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **10-g monofilament + vibration/pinprick/temperature**, ankle reflexes; inspect skin, deformity, pulses
Screen at type 2 diagnosis, 5 years after type 1 diagnosis, then at least annually
Check B12, TSH, renal function when evaluating neuropathy; consider serum electrophoresis if unexplained
Atypical pattern → nerve conduction studies; gastroparesis → exclude obstruction, gastric-emptying study
New third-nerve palsy → urgent vascular imaging; pupil sparing cannot reliably exclude aneurysm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pain → **duloxetine or pregabalin**; gabapentin or selected TCAs alternatives
Avoid TCAs with arrhythmia, urinary retention, frailty; avoid opioids for routine chronic neuropathic pain
Improve glycemic management; no drug reliably restores established sensory loss
Orthostasis → hydration, compression, medication review; persistent symptoms → midodrine
Gastroparesis → small low-fat meals, short-term metoclopramide; erectile dysfunction → sildenafil unless nitrates

rows.label: Complications
items: Painless ulcers, osteomyelitis, amputation, Charcot arthropathy
Falls, burns, painless MI; metoclopramide → tardive dyskinesia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection, protective footwear**, podiatry for callus/nail care; never walk barefoot
Regular foot exams, smoking cessation; warm swollen neuropathic foot → off-load and assess Charcot/infection

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: posterior column findings, elevated methylmalonic acid
Radiculopathy: dermatomal unilateral pain with root-specific weakness
Peripheral arterial disease: exertional pain, reduced pulses, ischemic skin changes

diabetic-neuropathy.evidence: Not checked online; established diabetes neuropathy screening and management teaching.

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Burning/numb feet, reduced vibration and ankle reflexes
Orthostasis, tachycardia, gastroparesis, bladder/sexual dysfunction, hypoglycemia unawareness
Acute isolated nerve deficit; often reversible

esophageal-motility-disorders.name: Esophageal motility disorders
esophageal-motility-disorders.scope: Achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm, hypercontractile esophagus, Zenker diverticulum, manometry, barium swallow
esophageal-motility-disorders.core: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset suggests impaired motility; progressive solids-first dysphagia suggests mechanical obstruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Achalasia often idiopathic; Chagas disease can destroy enteric ganglia
Older age predisposes to Zenker diverticulum; opioids can produce spastic motility patterns

rows.label: Clues
items: Achalasia: regurgitated undigested food, nocturnal cough, weight loss
★ Zenker: **halitosis, cervical gurgling, aspiration**, retained food hours after eating
Spastic disorders: intermittent dysphagia and squeezing chest pain; hot/cold liquids may provoke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons → impaired LES relaxation and absent peristalsis
Zenker: cricopharyngeal dysfunction → mucosal herniation through Killian triangle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Esophageal symptoms → **upper endoscopy** to exclude stricture/cancer before motility testing
★ **High-resolution manometry** confirms functional disorder after structural disease excluded
Barium swallow defines emptying; suspected Zenker → **barium study before endoscopy**
Rapid weight loss, older onset or difficult LES passage → evaluate pseudoachalasia with CT/endoscopic ultrasound
Chest pain → exclude ACS before labeling esophageal spasm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Achalasia → pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy + fundoplication, or **POEM**
Botulinum toxin for achalasia when procedural risk precludes durable treatment
Spastic disorders → remove opioid trigger, treat reflux; diltiazem or nitrates for persistent symptoms
Symptomatic Zenker → endoscopic septotomy/cricopharyngeal myotomy; avoid blind nasogastric instrumentation

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition; longstanding achalasia → increased squamous cancer risk
Dilation/myotomy → perforation; myotomy, especially POEM → gastroesophageal reflux

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, remain upright after meals to reduce regurgitation/aspiration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal cancer: progressive solids-first symptoms; obstructing lesion
Scleroderma: hypotensive LES with reflux, distal aperistalsis

table.title: Manometry and contrast findings
rows: Impaired LES relaxation; absent normal peristalsis

esophageal-motility-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG achalasia guideline](https://gi.org/guideline/diagnosis-and-management-of-achalasia/); other disorders established teaching.

gallstone-disease.name: Gallstone disease
gallstone-disease.scope: Biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis
gallstone-disease.core: Gallstone location determines the syndrome: transient cystic obstruction, gallbladder inflammation, common-duct obstruction/infection, or pancreatic inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss, ileal disease/resection
Hemolysis/cirrhosis → pigment stones; critical illness/TPN → acalculous cholecystitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Postprandial RUQ/epigastric discomfort radiating to back or right shoulder; assess fever and jaundice
★ **Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice** → cholangitis; hypotension/confusion → severe infection
Pancreatitis: persistent epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting; ALT >150 supports biliary cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cholesterol supersaturation or pigment precipitation creates calculi; obstruction location dictates organ injury
Infected obstructed bile ducts require drainage because antibiotics cannot reliably sterilize a closed system

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RUQ ultrasound first**; CBC, bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase, AST/ALT, lipase
Suspected cholecystitis with equivocal ultrasound → HIDA; nonvisualized gallbladder supports cystic-duct obstruction
Intermediate common-duct stone probability → MRCP or EUS; ERCP reserved primarily for treatment
★ Direct intervention: **stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL plus dilated duct**

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, fluids, antiemetics; infection → ceftriaxone/metronidazole or piperacillin/tazobactam
★ **Cholangitis → urgent biliary drainage**, immediately after stabilization if shock; do not await antibiotic response
Poor surgical candidate with acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy
★ Gallstone pancreatitis → supportive care, early oral feeding; **no urgent ERCP without cholangitis/persistent obstruction**

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, gangrene, perforation, abscess, septic shock; pancreatitis → necrosis/organ failure
Cholecystoenteric fistula → gallstone ileus; imaging: bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic stone
ERCP → pancreatitis/bleeding/perforation; cholecystectomy → bile-duct injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss; selected bariatric patients → ursodiol prophylaxis
After duct clearance → cholecystectomy; after mild biliary pancreatitis → same-admission cholecystectomy
Asymptomatic uncomplicated stones → observation; no routine prophylactic surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatitis: marked aminotransferase elevation, no obstructing stone
PUD: burning epigastric pain, ulcer on endoscopy
Inferior MI: ischemic ECG/troponin changes, cardiovascular risk

table.title: Localizing obstruction
rows: Persistent >6 hours, Murphy sign, wall thickening
Cholestatic labs, duct stone/dilation; no infection
ERCP extraction or operative duct clearance
Inflamed gallbladder without stones; critically ill

gastrointestinal-bleeding.name: Gastrointestinal bleeding
gastrointestinal-bleeding.scope: Upper GI bleeding (PUD, varices, Mallory-Weiss), lower GI bleeding (diverticular, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids), fluid and transfusion thresholds, endoscopy
gastrointestinal-bleeding.core: Hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia → assess hemodynamics before localizing; brisk upper bleeding can present as bright red rectal blood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NSAIDs/H pylori → ulcers; cirrhosis → varices; forceful retching → mucosal tear
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase severity; older age favors diverticula or angiodysplasia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Syncope, orthostasis, shock** signal major loss; initial hemoglobin may remain normal
Epigastric pain supports ulcer; painless bleeding favors vascular sources
Recurrent occult loss → iron deficiency; elevated BUN/creatinine ratio supports upper source

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal injury, portal-pressure collaterals, or fragile vessels rupture into GI lumen
Volume depletion → reduced perfusion; ongoing bleeding may require massive transfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Two large-bore IVs, CBC, type/cross, coagulation tests**, serial hemoglobin; resuscitate before procedures
Upper source → EGD within 24 hours after stabilization; suspected varices → within 12 hours
★ Ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia → **CT angiography → embolization** if active extravasation
Stable lower bleeding → bowel preparation and nonemergent colonoscopy; routine <24-hour colonoscopy adds no benefit

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crystalloid initially; stable nonischemic adults → **RBC transfusion at hemoglobin <7 g/dL**
Active exsanguination → blood immediately regardless of hemoglobin; cardiac ischemia → individualize higher threshold
Severe life-threatening anticoagulant bleeding → drug-specific reversal; persistent bleeding after endoscopy → IR/surgery
Suspected ulcer → IV PPI; endoscopic hemostasis for active bleeding/visible vessel, then high-dose PPI

rows.label: Complications
items: Rebleeding, aspiration, myocardial ischemia, AKI; variceal bleeding → infection
Massive transfusion → hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy; embolization → bowel ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H pylori and confirm cure; avoid NSAIDs; PPI for high-risk users
After variceal control: nonselective beta-blocker plus repeat banding; recurrent bleeding → TIPS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron/bismuth: dark stool without blood loss
Hemoptysis: coughing frothy blood rather than vomiting
Swallowed epistaxis: nasal source on examination

gastrointestinal-bleeding.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG lower GI bleeding 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36735555/), [ACS transfusion guidance 2025](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009).

genitourinary-trauma.name: Genitourinary trauma
genitourinary-trauma.scope: Posterior urethral injury, anterior urethral injury, bladder rupture, retrograde urethrography, renal trauma, testicular trauma
genitourinary-trauma.core: Hematuria or inability to void after trauma requires localization of urinary injury before instrumentation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pelvic fracture → posterior urethra/bladder; straddle injury → anterior bulbar urethra
Deceleration, flank impact or penetrating wounds → renal/collecting-system injury
Blunt scrotal trauma → testicular rupture; empty bladder better protected than distended bladder

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Blood at urethral meatus**, retention or perineal hematoma → urethral injury
Gross hematuria with pelvic fracture → suspect bladder rupture
Flank ecchymosis, tenderness or lower rib fractures suggest renal injury
Scrotal swelling, bruising and loss of normal contour suggest testicular rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pelvic shearing disrupts membranous urethra; direct compression splits the bulbar segment
Intraperitoneal urine leakage irritates peritoneum; blood loss can cause shock despite modest hematuria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected urethral injury → **retrograde urethrogram before Foley**; no blind repeated attempts
★ Stable gross hematuria + pelvic fracture → **retrograde CT/plain cystography**
Renal concern, stable → contrast CT abdomen/pelvis with delayed images; microscopic hematuria plus hypotension qualifies
Normal hematuria assessment cannot exclude renal vascular injury after high-energy deceleration
Testicular injury → Doppler ultrasound; high clinical suspicion should not delay exploration

rows.label: Tx
items: Hemodynamic instability → trauma resuscitation and urgent operative/angiographic hemorrhage control
Urethral disruption → urology, suprapubic drainage or selected endoscopic realignment
★ **Intraperitoneal bladder rupture → surgical repair**; uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture → catheter drainage
Stable renal injuries → observation; ongoing arterial bleeding → selective embolization
Testicular rupture → urgent exploration, repair and removal of nonviable tissue

rows.label: Complications
items: Urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction, incontinence; urinary extravasation → infection or urinoma
Delayed renal bleeding, hypertension or kidney loss; testicular atrophy and infertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective equipment; safe catheter technique; follow-up for stricture after urethral injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: absent flow with spermatic-cord twist; also surgical emergency
Nontraumatic stone: colicky flank pain without injury mechanism

head-and-neck-cancer.name: Head and neck cancer
head-and-neck-cancer.scope: Oral cavity cancer, laryngeal cancer, pharyngeal cancer, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, tobacco and alcohol risk, HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma
head-and-neck-cancer.core: Persistent hoarseness, unilateral throat/ear symptoms, a nonhealing oral lesion, or an adult neck mass requires malignancy evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Tobacco plus alcohol synergistically increase squamous cancer risk; betel nut in some populations
HPV exposure drives many oropharyngeal cancers; EBV associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma

rows.label: Clues
items: Oral ulcer or red/white plaque persisting >2–3 weeks; dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss
★ **Adult persistent lateral neck mass** may be metastatic carcinoma, even when cystic
Unilateral referred otalgia with normal otoscopy; hemoptysis or stridor indicates advanced local disease
Nasopharyngeal disease → unilateral serous otitis, epistaxis or cranial neuropathy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal squamous transformation and lymphatic spread; field carcinogenesis produces synchronous/second primary tumors

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Direct visualization and biopsy** of mucosal lesion; flexible nasolaryngoscopy for inaccessible sites
Neck mass → contrast CT/MRI plus **fine-needle aspiration**; avoid initial open biopsy
Oropharyngeal tumor → p16/HPV testing; staging imaging assesses regional nodes and distant metastases
Persistent hoarseness → laryngoscopy; no prolonged empiric reflux treatment when malignancy clues present

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway compromise/stridor → **secure airway** with ENT/anesthesia support
Early localized cancer → surgery or radiation according to site and function
Locally advanced → combined surgery/radiation with cisplatin-based systemic treatment or definitive chemoradiation
Nasopharyngeal cancer → chemoradiation; recurrent/metastatic disease → systemic treatment, often checkpoint inhibitor

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, airway obstruction, malnutrition, carotid bleeding; nodal/distant metastases
Radiation → xerostomia, dental decay, osteoradionecrosis; surgery → speech/swallow impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Smoking/alcohol cessation, HPV vaccination; dental assessment before head/neck radiation
Swallowing rehabilitation, nutrition support; surveillance for recurrence and second primary cancer

rows.label: Mimics
items: Laryngitis: brief postviral hoarseness resolving with recovery
Branchial cleft cyst: benign developmental lesion; new adult cystic mass still needs cancer exclusion

head-and-neck-cancer.evidence: Neck-mass evaluation checked 2026-10-30: [AAO-HNS adult neck-mass guideline](https://www.entnet.org/quality-practice/quality-products/clinical-practice-guidelines/evaluation-of-the-neck-mass-in-adults/); oncology: established teaching.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.scope: HFrEF, HFpEF, acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic flash pulmonary edema, guideline-directed medical therapy, neurohormonal activation (RAAS, ADH-mediated hyponatremia)
heart-failure.core: Inadequate cardiac output or elevated filling pressures → pulmonary or systemic congestion, even with a normal ejection fraction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CAD, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy
Decompensation triggers: ischemia, infection, arrhythmia, missed diuretics, NSAIDs

rows.label: Clues
items: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated JVP, crackles, dependent edema
S3 suggests volume overload; S4 suggests stiff ventricle
★ **Flash edema**: abrupt respiratory distress, severe hypertension, pink frothy sputum

rows.label: Pathophys
items: RAAS/sympathetic activation → vasoconstriction, sodium retention, adverse remodeling
Nonosmotic **ADH** release → dilutional hyponatremia; marker of advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography**: EF, valves, wall motion; ECG, CXR, BNP support diagnosis
Low BNP argues against HF; obesity lowers BNP, renal dysfunction raises it
Identify precipitant: troponin, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine; evaluate ischemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute congestion → **IV furosemide**; hypoxemia → oxygen; respiratory distress → noninvasive ventilation
★ Hypertensive pulmonary edema → **IV nitroglycerin**; shock → norepinephrine ± dobutamine, urgent cause correction
Start beta-blocker only when compensated; ACE inhibitor → ARNI requires 36-hour washout
MRA requires eGFR >30, K <5; persistent EF ≤35% despite GDMT → consider ICD

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiorenal syndrome, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death, hepatic congestion
Diuresis → hypokalemia; RAAS blockade → hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction; monitor creatinine/K

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily weights, sodium moderation, adherence; **continue GDMT after EF recovery**
Treat hypertension, CAD, AF; smoking cessation, exercise, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: COPD: obstructive spirometry, hyperinflation
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia
PE: pleuritic pain, thrombotic risk, RV strain

heart-failure.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACC HFrEF 2024](https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/03/06/19/22/2024-acc-expert-consensus-hfref); other points established teaching.

humeral-fractures.name: Humeral fractures
humeral-fractures.scope: Proximal humerus fracture (axillary nerve), humeral shaft fracture (radial nerve, wrist drop), neurologic assessment, coaptation splint, functional brace, surgical fixation indications
humeral-fractures.core: Humeral fracture management depends on location, displacement, and neurovascular injury; document nerve function before and after manipulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older adults with osteoporosis: low-energy proximal fractures; younger adults: high-energy trauma
Shaft injuries from direct blow, twisting, falls; consider malignancy with minimal-trauma shaft fracture

rows.label: Clues
items: Upper-arm pain, swelling, ecchymosis, deformity; reduced shoulder/elbow motion
★ Proximal/surgical neck injury → **axillary nerve**: lateral shoulder numbness, impaired deltoid function
★ Shaft injury → **radial nerve**: wrist/finger extension weakness, dorsal first-web-space sensory loss
Cold pulseless hand, expanding hematoma, severe stretch pain → urgent vascular/compartment evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Axillary nerve wraps around surgical neck; radial nerve travels along the spiral groove
Closed-fracture radial palsy often reflects neurapraxia and recovers without immediate exploration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AP/lateral humerus radiographs including shoulder and elbow**; dedicated joint views when involved
Check pulses, capillary refill, motor/sensory function of radial, median, ulnar, and axillary nerves
Repeat examination after reduction/splinting; CT for complex proximal/articular fracture planning
Open wound near fracture → evaluate as open fracture even if bone not visible

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, immobilization, ice; open injury → IV cefazolin, tetanus protection, urgent irrigation/debridement
★ Most closed shaft fractures → **coaptation splint**, then functional brace after swelling subsides
Minimally displaced proximal fracture → sling, early supervised range of motion to limit stiffness
Displaced complex proximal patterns → fixation or selected arthroplasty depending on age and reconstructability
★ Surgery: **open fracture, vascular injury, floating elbow**, unacceptable alignment, failed bracing/nonunion

rows.label: Complications
items: Radial nerve palsy, malunion/nonunion; proximal injuries: avascular necrosis, shoulder stiffness
Secondary/new palsy after reduction or penetrating injury → urgent specialist reassessment, possible exploration

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall reduction, osteoporosis evaluation after fragility fracture; rehabilitation preserves joint motion
No prolonged unmonitored sling use; regular alignment and neurovascular follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Shoulder dislocation: altered contour and displaced humeral head on joint views
Rotator cuff tear: weakness without fracture, especially persistent after healing

humeral-fractures.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic teaching.

hypercalcemia.name: Hypercalcemia
hypercalcemia.scope: Primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, milk-alkali syndrome, IV saline resuscitation, calcitonin, bisphosphonates
hypercalcemia.core: Elevated calcium causes stones, constipation, polyuria, weakness, and neuropsychiatric changes; PTH distinguishes hormone-driven disease from other causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Parathyroid adenoma/hyperplasia, malignancy, prolonged immobilization
Thiazides, lithium, excess vitamin D or calcium/absorbable alkali, granulomatous disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Dehydration, nausea, abdominal pain, reduced reflexes; ECG may show shortened QT
★ **Calcium >14 mg/dL**, confusion, arrhythmia, or severe volume depletion → urgent treatment
Primary hyperparathyroidism often asymptomatic; malignancy-associated disease tends to progress rapidly

rows.label: Pathophys
items: PTH promotes bone resorption and renal calcium retention while increasing phosphate excretion
Hypercalcemia impairs renal concentration → dehydration, reduced calcium clearance, self-reinforcing elevation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm with repeat total/albumin-adjusted or **ionized calcium**, especially with altered proteins or critical illness
★ **Intact PTH first**; elevated or inappropriately normal → PTH-dependent
Suppressed PTH → PTHrP, vitamin D metabolites, malignancy/myeloma evaluation guided by context
Primary disease versus FHH → urine calcium; clearance ratio <0.01 favors FHH, with overlap
Parathyroid imaging localizes before surgery; never establishes biochemical diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe/symptomatic → **IV isotonic saline**, then calcitonin for rapid temporary lowering
★ **IV zoledronic acid** for sustained malignancy control; denosumab if severe renal limitations/refractory disease
Calcitriol-mediated disease → glucocorticoids; dialysis for refractory life-threatening elevation or inability to hydrate
Primary disease: surgery for symptoms, age <50, calcium >1 above ULN, osteoporosis/fracture, stones, eGFR <60
Stop causative supplements/drugs; loop diuretic only for fluid overload, not routine calcium elimination

rows.label: Complications
items: Nephrolithiasis, nephrocalcinosis, AKI, osteoporosis/fractures, pancreatitis
Calcitonin tachyphylaxis after 48–72 hours; antiresorptives can cause hypocalcemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hydration, avoid excess calcium/alkali; monitor calcium, renal function, and bone density when observing primary disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: FHH: lifelong mild elevation, family history, hypocalciuria; surgery ineffective
Pseudohypercalcemia: high protein-bound calcium but normal ionized fraction

hypercalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established calcium evaluation and emergency management.

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine; postoperative pain, nausea, endurance exercise
Pulmonary/CNS disease, malignancy; heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
Hypovolemia → isotonic saline; SIADH → fluid restriction, increased solute, remove trigger
Edematous states → fluid/sodium restriction and loop diuretic; treat heart/liver/kidney disorder
★ Chronic/unknown duration: generally limit rise to **≤8 mEq/L per 24 h**; monitor frequently
Overcorrection → desmopressin plus D5W; avoid routine vaptans in acute symptomatic cases

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute severe hyponatremia → herniation, respiratory arrest
Osmotic demyelination after rapid correction; greatest risk with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids during high ADH states; review causative drugs
Monitor for brisk aquaresis after restoring volume or stopping thiazides

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemia: measured osmolality elevated
Primary psychiatric disease: neurologic change without sodium abnormality

hyponatremia.evidence: Not checked online; established hyponatremia consensus principles.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.scope: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis), toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, biologic therapy
inflammatory-bowel-disease.core: Chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation: Crohn disease affects any gastrointestinal segment; ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, young adulthood; smoking worsens Crohn disease
NSAIDs and enteric infections can precipitate flares

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia; children may have growth failure
Arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum; PSC particularly associated with UC
★ Severe colitis: fever, tachycardia, frequent bloody stools; distention suggests **toxic megacolon**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysregulated mucosal immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stool **C. difficile** testing and cultures before attributing worsening diarrhea to inflammation
Fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation; **ileocolonoscopy with biopsies** confirms
Suspected small-bowel disease or abscess → MR enterography; avoid capsule with suspected stricture
Fulminant colitis → abdominal radiograph and limited sigmoidoscopy; avoid full colonoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe UC → hospitalization, **IV methylprednisolone**, fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Steroid-refractory severe UC → infliximab or cyclosporine; perforation or megacolon → urgent colectomy
★ Steroids induce remission only; **never maintenance**
Crohn abscess → antibiotics and drainage before immunosuppression

rows.label: Complications
items: Fistulas, strictures, obstruction and B12 deficiency in Crohn; colectomy does not cure Crohn
Colonic disease → colorectal cancer; active inflammation → venous thromboembolism

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Colonic disease → surveillance colonoscopy beginning about **8 years** after onset; PSC → immediately
Vaccinate and screen TB/HBV before biologics; smoking cessation for Crohn

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory markers
Ischemic colitis: abrupt pain followed by hematochezia, vascular risk

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate, reason, communicate choice**; specific to decision, fluctuating
Competence: legal determination; diagnosis, age, or disagreement alone does not establish incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, including life-saving treatment; avoid coercion or abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no available surrogate/directive → implied consent for necessary treatment
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or substantially changed risk → renewed consent discussion

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

inguinal-hernia.name: Inguinal hernia
inguinal-hernia.scope: Direct inguinal hernia, indirect inguinal hernia, femoral hernia, incarcerated and strangulated hernia, physical exam, elective vs emergent surgical repair
inguinal-hernia.core: A groin bulge enlarging with strain suggests hernia; a painful irreducible mass with obstructive or ischemic signs requires urgent surgical assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Male sex, family history, prematurity, persistent processus vaginalis
Age-related fascial weakness, chronic cough, constipation, heavy strain; femoral hernias more frequent in women

rows.label: Clues
items: Bulge or dragging discomfort with standing/Valsalva, improving supine or after reduction
Incarcerated: contents cannot be reduced; bowel obstruction causes vomiting, distention, obstipation
★ **Severe persistent pain**, tenderness, erythema, toxicity/peritonitis → impaired perfusion; fever may be late

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abdominal contents protrude through a weak opening; a narrow neck impairs venous then arterial perfusion
Richter hernia traps only bowel-wall segment; ischemia may occur without complete obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Standing groin examination with cough/Valsalva**; inspect both sides and assess reducibility
Uncertain occult lesion → dynamic ultrasound; CT if obstruction, complication, or alternative diagnosis suspected
Clinical strangulation → immediate operation; imaging must not delay treatment
Do not rely on surface examination alone to reliably distinguish direct from indirect anatomy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Strangulation → **IV fluids, NPO, analgesia, antibiotics, emergency repair**; resect nonviable bowel
Incarceration without ischemic features → urgent surgeon evaluation; gentle reduction only in selected cases
★ Symptomatic inguinal hernia → **elective mesh repair** in adults; children → herniotomy
Minimally symptomatic men may choose watchful waiting with return precautions
Women and femoral hernias → timely repair because occult femoral disease and strangulation risk are greater

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel obstruction, ischemic necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Repair → chronic groin pain, recurrence, wound/mesh infection, testicular ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat constipation and chronic cough, smoking cessation, weight management; risk reduction cannot close an existing defect
After reduction or observation: urgent return for escalating pain, vomiting, or loss of reducibility

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lymphadenopathy: discrete solid nodes without cough impulse
Hydrocele: transilluminates; confined fluid rather than reducible bowel
Saphena varix: compressible venous swelling; Doppler demonstrates venous flow

table.title: Anatomic distinctions
rows: Below inguinal ligament, medial femoral vein

intussusception.name: Intussusception
intussusception.scope: Idiopathic ileocolic intussusception, pathologic lead points (Meckel, polyp), target sign on ultrasound, air enema
intussusception.core: Bowel telescoping causes intermittent obstruction and ischemia, often in a previously healthy infant with episodic distress and deceptively well intervals.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually age 6–36 months; lymphoid hyperplasia after viral illness
Older child, recurrent episode or adult → pathologic lead point: Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Sudden recurrent **colicky pain with knees drawn up**, pallor and vomiting
Lethargy can dominate; bilious emesis or distention suggests progressing obstruction
Sausage-shaped RUQ mass, empty RLQ; currant-jelly stool is late and often absent
Shock, guarding, fever or peritonitis → compromised bowel/perforation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Proximal bowel and mesentery invaginate distally → venous congestion, edema and arterial ischemia
Ileocolic location most common in children; bleeding reflects injured mucosa

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal ultrasound first** → target/doughnut on transverse view, pseudokidney longitudinally
Plain radiograph for obstruction/free air when severe findings; normal radiograph does not exclude
CT generally for adult cases or uncertain alternative diagnosis, not routine pediatric first test
Classic clinical triad uncommon; do not delay testing until bloody stools appear

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV fluids**, analgesia; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Stable without peritonitis/perforation → **air or contrast enema reduction** with surgical backup
Failed reduction, perforation, shock or peritonitis → urgent surgery; resect nonviable bowel
Persistent/recurrent disease or suspected lead point → surgical evaluation; adult cases usually require resection

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, shock; recurrence after successful reduction
Enema-associated perforation → immediate surgical management

rows.label: Prevention
items: No usual primary prevention for idiopathic disease; remove identified pathologic lead point
After reduction → observe recovery, resume intake when tolerated; counsel on recurrent episodic symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: diarrhea predominates, less discrete symptom-free intervals
Malrotation/volvulus: bilious vomiting in neonate, urgent surgical evaluation

invasive-fungal-infections.name: Invasive fungal infections
invasive-fungal-infections.scope: Invasive aspergillosis, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), mucormycosis, candidemia, amphotericin B, voriconazole, systemic corticosteroids
invasive-fungal-infections.core: Fungal syndromes range from allergic airway disease to lethal tissue invasion; immune status and imaging guide testing and treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prolonged neutropenia/transplant → molds; DKA, glucocorticoids or iron overload → mucormycosis
Central lines, TPN, abdominal surgery, broad antibiotics → invasive Candida
ABPA: asthma or cystic fibrosis; hypersensitivity rather than tissue invasion

rows.label: Clues
items: Invasive aspergillosis: fever despite antibiotics, pleuritic pain, hemoptysis, pulmonary nodules
★ **Black nasal/palatal eschar**, facial pain, ophthalmoplegia → rhinocerebral mucormycosis
Candidemia: sepsis, persistent positive blood cultures; metastatic eye, heart or deep-organ infection
ABPA: recurrent wheeze, brown mucus plugs, fleeting pulmonary infiltrates

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Angioinvasive molds cause vascular thrombosis, infarction and necrosis
Candida translocates through damaged gut or colonizes intravascular devices, then disseminates hematogenously

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected mold pneumonia → **chest CT**, bronchoscopy/BAL or tissue biopsy
Aspergillus galactomannan in serum/BAL; β-D-glucan supports several fungi but usually negative in mucormycosis
Necrotic sinus lesion → urgent endoscopic biopsy for histology/culture; do not await blood cultures
Candidemia → repeat blood cultures until clear; assess source and metastatic foci
ABPA: Aspergillus-IgE + total IgE ≥500 IU/mL; two of eosinophilia, Aspergillus-IgG, CT bronchiectasis/infiltrates

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Aspergillosis → **voriconazole** or isavuconazole; evaluate interactions and liver function
★ Mucormycosis → **liposomal amphotericin B + urgent surgical debridement**; correct DKA/immunosuppression
Candidemia → echinocandin such as micafungin; step down to fluconazole when stable, susceptible and cleared
Remove implicated line when feasible; uncomplicated candidemia → ≥14 days after clearance and symptom resolution
ABPA → prednisolone or itraconazole; recurrent flares → both; avoid steroids for untreated invasive disease

rows.label: Complications
items: CNS dissemination, massive hemoptysis, blindness, endocarditis; high mortality if treatment delayed
Amphotericin → AKI, hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia; voriconazole → visual effects, hepatotoxicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: Selected high-risk prolonged neutropenia → posaconazole prophylaxis; line hygiene and antibiotic stewardship

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pseudomonas ecthyma gangrenosum: necrotic skin lesions with bacterial sepsis
Bacterial abscess: pyogenic cultures; malignancy: tissue without invasive organisms

lung-cancer.name: Lung cancer
lung-cancer.scope: Non-small cell, small cell, paraneoplastic syndromes, Pancoast, screening
lung-cancer.core: Persistent cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, or a suspicious lung lesion requires tissue diagnosis and staging before treatment selection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, radon, asbestos, occupational carcinogens, prior thoracic radiation; adenocarcinoma also occurs in never-smokers

rows.label: Clues
items: Recurrent focal pneumonia, hoarseness, clubbing, unexplained pleural effusion
★ **Pancoast tumor**: shoulder/ulnar-arm pain + ipsilateral Horner syndrome
SVC obstruction: facial swelling, neck-vein distention; cord compression or airway compromise requires urgent action

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Bronchogenic malignant transformation → local invasion, lymphatic spread, hematogenous metastasis
Ectopic hormone production and immune cross-reactivity cause paraneoplastic syndromes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspicious finding → **contrast chest CT**; biopsy easiest site that establishes highest stage
Central lesion/nodes → bronchoscopy/EBUS; peripheral lesion → CT-guided biopsy; effusion → cytology
PET/CT for extracranial staging, brain MRI for selected stages/small-cell disease; pulmonary function before resection
Molecular profiling and PD-L1 guide advanced NSCLC treatment; suspicious nodes often require pathologic staging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early operable NSCLC → **surgical resection + nodal evaluation**; inoperable localized → stereotactic radiation
Locally advanced NSCLC → combined systemic treatment/radiation ± surgery in selected patients
Metastatic NSCLC → biomarker-directed agents or immunotherapy/chemotherapy
★ Small-cell → **platinum + etoposide**, stage-dependent radiation/immunotherapy; surgery rarely used

rows.label: Complications
items: Brain/bone/adrenal/liver metastases, malignant effusion, thrombosis, respiratory failure
Radiation pneumonitis; checkpoint inhibitors → immune pneumonitis/endocrinopathies

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **annual low-dose CT**, age 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, current smoking or quit <15 years
Stop after 15 quit-years or limited curative candidacy; **ACS omits quit-time restriction**
Smoking cessation and radon mitigation; chest radiographs do not substitute for screening CT

rows.label: Mimics
items: TB/fungal granuloma: microbiologic evidence; PET uptake not specific for cancer
Hamartoma: fat/popcorn calcification; pneumonia: clinical/radiographic response to antibiotics

lung-cancer.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF 2021](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening), [ACS 2023 guideline](https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.3322/caac.21811); treatment: established stage-based framework.

necrotizing-enterocolitis.name: Necrotizing enterocolitis
necrotizing-enterocolitis.scope: Prematurity, formula feeding, abdominal distention, pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, pneumoperitoneum, bowel rest, emergent exploratory laparotomy
necrotizing-enterocolitis.core: A vulnerable newborn develops feeding intolerance and systemic deterioration; intestinal wall gas establishes bowel injury requiring immediate medical and surgical evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Prematurity**, very low birth weight, formula feeding; human milk protective
Term infants: impaired intestinal perfusion from congenital heart disease or perinatal illness

rows.label: Clues
items: Abdominal distention, bilious residuals/emesis, hematochezia, reduced bowel sounds
Temperature instability, apnea, lethargy, bradycardia may precede obvious abdominal findings
★ Abdominal wall erythema/discoloration, peritonitis, shock → advanced disease
Thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidosis, rising lactate support progression

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immature intestinal barrier + dysbiosis + inflammation → mucosal injury and bacterial invasion
Progressive necrosis may become transmural; bacterial gas enters bowel wall and portal circulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Abdominal radiograph: **pneumatosis intestinalis**; portal venous gas supports diagnosis
Supine plus decubitus/cross-table imaging assesses free air; ultrasound evaluates perfusion and free fluid
CBC/platelets, electrolytes, blood gas/lactate, cultures; serial examinations and imaging track evolution
Early films may show only ileus; absence of pneumatosis does not exclude early NEC

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO + NG/OG decompression**, IV fluids, cardiorespiratory support, early pediatric surgical consultation
IV ampicillin + gentamicin ± metronidazole for advanced disease; alternative: piperacillin-tazobactam
Parenteral nutrition during bowel rest; correct electrolyte disturbances, coagulopathy, anemia
★ **Pneumoperitoneum**, peritonitis, or deterioration despite treatment → emergency exploration and necrotic bowel resection
Extremely unstable infant: peritoneal drainage may temporize; reassess need for laparotomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Sepsis, DIC, perforation, death; later intestinal strictures and obstruction
Extensive resection → short bowel syndrome, malabsorption, parenteral-nutrition-associated cholestasis
Growth impairment and neurodevelopmental disability among survivors

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Mother's milk or donor human milk; structured neonatal feeding protocols
Avoid unnecessary prolonged antibiotics and acid suppression; routine probiotics lack universal US recommendation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Spontaneous intestinal perforation: isolated perforation, often earlier, without diffuse pneumatosis
Malrotation/volvulus: sudden bilious emesis; urgent evaluation even with initially benign examination
Milk protein proctocolitis: bloody stools in otherwise well, growing infant

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.scope: Acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
pancreatitis.core: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with pancreatic inflammation may be acute; repeated injury produces irreversible chronic insufficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gallstones, alcohol, triglycerides >1,000 mg/dL, ERCP, hypercalcemia, medications
Chronic: prolonged alcohol/tobacco exposure, genetic disease, duct obstruction, autoimmune disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Severe constant pain, vomiting, tenderness, ileus; chronic disease adds steatorrhea and weight loss
★ **Hypoxemia, hypotension, oliguria, persistent SIRS** → early monitored/ICU assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature intrapancreatic enzyme activation → autodigestion and systemic inflammation
Chronic fibrosis destroys acinar/islet tissue; lipase may normalize despite advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute diagnosis: **2 of 3**—typical pain, lipase ≥3× ULN, characteristic imaging
RUQ ultrasound evaluates gallstones; triglycerides, calcium, liver tests identify cause
Contrast CT for uncertain diagnosis, deterioration, or failure to improve after 48–72 hours; not routine immediately
Chronic: CT/MRCP shows calcification/duct changes; fecal elastase <200 supports exocrine insufficiency

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute: **moderate lactated Ringer resuscitation**, frequent reassessment, analgesia, electrolyte correction; avoid overload
★ **Early oral low-fat feeding** within 24–48 hours if tolerated; enteral tube feeding if unable
Biliary with cholangitis → urgent ERCP; mild gallstone disease → cholecystectomy before discharge
Sterile necrosis: no antibiotics; infected: penetrating antibiotics, delayed step-up drainage/debridement
Chronic: stop alcohol/tobacco; pancreatic enzymes, nutrition/fat-soluble vitamins, pain and diabetes management

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, AKI, shock, hypocalcemia; local necrosis, vascular thrombosis, hemorrhage
Pseudocyst after >4 weeks; infected collection, obstruction; chronic disease → pancreatic cancer and brittle diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Treat cause**: gallbladder removal, triglyceride control, avoid culprit drug and alcohol
Post-ERCP rectal indomethacin in eligible patients; selected pancreatic duct stenting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Perforated ulcer: rigid abdomen/free air
Mesenteric ischemia: pain-exam mismatch; MI: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern

table.title: Severity and collections
rows: Transient dysfunction ≤48 hours or local complication

perioperative-care.name: Perioperative care
perioperative-care.scope: Preoperative cardiac risk, pulmonary evaluation, surgical antibiotic prophylaxis, medication management, pain control
perioperative-care.core: Optimize active disease, estimate procedural and patient risk, and order testing only when the result could change perioperative management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Emergency, vascular or intrathoracic surgery; ischemic heart disease, heart failure, CKD, diabetes
Smoking, COPD, OSA, frailty, malnutrition and prior anesthesia complications

rows.label: Clues
items: Chest pain, new dyspnea, syncope or decompensated fluid overload require targeted evaluation
Poor functional capacity: inability to climb stairs or perform activities around 4 METs

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Surgical stress raises myocardial oxygen demand; anesthesia can lower perfusion pressure
Sedation, pain and recumbency reduce ventilation and promote atelectasis and venous stasis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RCRI/NSQIP** plus functional assessment; no routine stress test for low-risk surgery
Selected elevated-risk surgery with poor/unknown capacity → stress test only if results change management
ECG for cardiovascular symptoms; echo for new/worsening HF or suspected significant valve disease
No routine chest radiograph/spirometry without respiratory findings; assess airway and OSA history

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Active ACS, decompensated HF or unstable arrhythmia → defer elective surgery and stabilize
★ Continue chronic **beta blockers/statins**; do not start beta blockade on surgery day
Hold **SGLT2 inhibitors 3–4 days**; individualize GLP-1 drugs by aspiration risk; continue reduced basal insulin
★ **Cefazolin within 60 minutes** before incision; vancomycin infusion starts within 120 minutes
Multimodal analgesia: acetaminophen, regional block, selective NSAID; opioids for breakthrough, respiratory monitoring

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial injury, AKI, delirium, pneumonia, VTE and surgical-site infection
Opioids aggravate OSA; excessive fluids can worsen pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, lung expansion exercises, early mobilization, mechanical/pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis
Anticoagulation interruption individualized; bridging reserved for highest thrombotic risk
Chronic steroid exposure with adrenal suppression → perioperative glucocorticoid coverage

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anxiety-related dyspnea: normal cardiopulmonary evaluation
Stable chronic disease: baseline symptoms alone do not mandate cancellation

pleural-effusion.name: Pleural effusion
pleural-effusion.scope: Transudate vs exudate (Light criteria), parapneumonic effusion, empyema, malignant effusion
pleural-effusion.core: Fluid in the pleural space causes dyspnea, dullness, and reduced breath sounds; classify by mechanism and identify infection requiring drainage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome; pneumonia, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, TB
Recent thoracic surgery, pancreatitis, esophageal rupture, autoimmune disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Pleuritic pain, reduced tactile fremitus; large effusion may shift mediastinum away
Fever or persistent sepsis despite antibiotics suggests complicated parapneumonic fluid
Bloody fluid suggests malignancy, embolism, or trauma; milky fluid suggests chyle

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transudate: altered hydrostatic/oncotic pressure; exudate: increased permeability or impaired lymphatic drainage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Chest radiograph → **ultrasound-guided thoracentesis** for new unexplained, unilateral, or atypical effusion
Classic bilateral heart-failure effusions → diuresis first; sample if fever, asymmetry, or treatment failure
★ **Exudate if any Light criterion** positive; compare paired pleural and serum measurements
Pleural pH, glucose, cell differential, Gram stain/culture; cytology if cancer suspected
Diuresis can create pseudoexudate; serum–pleural albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL supports transudate

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat systemic cause; therapeutic thoracentesis for significant symptoms; avoid rapid excessive drainage
★ Pus, positive culture, or **pH ≤7.20** → chest tube plus antibiotics
Loculated infected fluid → intrapleural tPA/DNase; persistent sepsis → VATS evaluation
★ Recurrent symptomatic malignancy → **indwelling pleural catheter** or pleurodesis; trapped lung favors catheter

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, loculation, trapped lung, respiratory compromise
Thoracentesis → pneumothorax, bleeding, reexpansion pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Heart-failure control, prompt pneumonia treatment; ultrasound guidance reduces procedural injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atelectasis: mediastinal shift toward volume loss
Consolidation: increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds
Pneumothorax: hyperresonance rather than dullness

pleural-effusion.evidence: Not checked online; established pleural disease teaching.

shock.name: Shock
shock.scope: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), obstructive, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors
shock.core: Circulatory failure causing tissue hypoperfusion; normal blood pressure does not exclude early shock.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemorrhage, GI losses, MI, infection, allergen exposure, spinal injury, thromboembolism
Recent surgery, immunosuppression, indwelling devices increase occult infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, altered mentation, oliguria, cool mottled skin; distributive forms may initially feel warm
★ **Anaphylaxis**: rapid airway swelling, wheezing, hypotension; skin findings may be absent
Neurogenic: hypotension with **bradycardia**, warm skin after spinal cord injury

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen delivery falls below demand → anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation
Distributive vasodilation → relative hypovolemia despite normal total body fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside ultrasound**: cardiac function, pericardial fluid, RV dilation, lung sliding, volume assessment
Serial lactate, capillary refill, urine output; CBC, chemistry, ECG, troponin; cultures if infection suspected
Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite volume resuscitation

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway/oxygen, IV access; **balanced crystalloid**, dynamic fluid-response reassessment; restrict with pulmonary congestion
★ Hemorrhage → **control bleeding + balanced blood products**; avoid large crystalloid loads
★ Septic shock → antibiotics within 1 hour, drainage/debridement; crystalloid 30 mL/kg within 3 hours
★ Persistent septic hypotension → **norepinephrine**, MAP ≥65; add vasopressin, then epinephrine; refractory → hydrocortisone

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, ischemic hepatitis, DIC, ARDS, bowel ischemia, multiorgan failure
Excess fluids → edema; vasopressors → digital/mesenteric ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early infection treatment, catheter hygiene, VTE prophylaxis, hemorrhage control
After anaphylaxis: trigger avoidance, epinephrine autoinjector, allergy referral

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal syncope: transient bradycardia, rapid recovery supine
Hypoglycemia: low bedside glucose, improvement with dextrose

table.title: Hemodynamics and cause-directed rescue
rows: Decompress pneumothorax; drain tamponade; reperfuse PE

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.name: Skin and soft tissue infections
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.scope: Cellulitis, erysipelas, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, lymphangitis, necrotizing fasciitis
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.core: Skin infection management depends on purulence, systemic illness, and signs of deep tissue destruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Skin breaks, tinea pedis, edema/lymphedema, diabetes, obesity, injection drug use
Prior MRSA, crowding, recent hospitalization; surgery or penetrating trauma raises deep-infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Warmth, tenderness, erythema; rapidly expanding margins or systemic toxicity require urgent reassessment
★ **Pain out of proportion**, bullae, anesthesia, crepitus, shock → necrotizing infection
Perineal involvement → Fournier gangrene; saltwater exposure → Vibrio, freshwater → Aeromonas

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nonpurulent infection usually streptococcal; purulent lesions usually S aureus
Fascial spread and toxin-mediated injury → thrombosis, necrosis, sepsis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical diagnosis; **bedside ultrasound** if occult fluid collection suspected
Culture drained pus for severe, recurrent, or resistant infection; blood cultures for systemic toxicity
Suspected necrotizing disease → immediate surgical evaluation; imaging must not delay exploration
Low laboratory risk score or absent gas does not exclude necrotizing fasciitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Deep infection → **urgent debridement + vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam**, add clindamycin for toxin suppression
Confirmed group A streptococcal necrotizing infection → penicillin + clindamycin
Severe cellulitis/systemic illness → IV cefazolin; MRSA risk → vancomycin
★ Abscess: add **antibiotics** for systemic signs, immunocompromise, extensive disease, or failed drainage

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacteremia, osteomyelitis, septic thrombophlebitis; tissue loss and amputation
Toxic shock, multiorgan failure; recurrent cellulitis worsens lymphatic dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat interdigital fungal infection, manage edema, skin hygiene, protect wounds
Recurrent staphylococcal infections → consider nasal mupirocin + chlorhexidine decolonization; avoid shared razors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Stasis dermatitis: chronic, often bilateral, itchy
DVT: deep swelling without superficial spreading infection; contact dermatitis: pruritic exposure-pattern rash

table.title: Superficial patterns
rows: Incision and drainage; TMP-SMX if needed

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established IDSA-based infection management.

skin-cancer.name: Skin cancer
skin-cancer.scope: Actinic keratosis, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, melanoma, photoprotection and sunscreen
skin-cancer.core: Changing pigmented lesions or persistent keratinizing, pearly, or ulcerated growths require examination and tissue diagnosis rather than empiric reassurance.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: UV exposure, fair skin, sunburns, tanning beds, older age; immunosuppression particularly increases SCC
Melanoma: numerous/atypical nevi, family/personal melanoma history; may arise without a preexisting nevus
Chronic wounds/scars predispose SCC; acral melanoma occurs regardless of skin pigmentation

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Melanoma: **ABCDE**—asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter, evolution; ugly-duckling lesion
Diameter >6 mm concerning, but smaller evolving lesions still require biopsy
Amelanotic melanoma may be pink; inspect soles, palms, nail beds; nail pigment extending onto fold concerning
Rapid growth, bleeding, nonhealing ulcer, fixation, neurologic symptoms, nodes → aggressive or advanced disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: UV-induced DNA damage → keratinocyte malignancy; melanocyte transformation causes melanoma
AK represents dysplastic keratinocytes with potential progression to invasive SCC

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspicious melanoma → **full-thickness excisional biopsy with narrow margins** to measure Breslow depth
Partial biopsy acceptable when complete excision impractical; avoid superficial sampling that prevents staging
Suspected keratinocyte carcinoma → shave, punch, or excisional biopsy deep enough to assess invasion
Breslow thickness/ulceration guide melanoma staging; sentinel-node discussion generally at ≥0.8 mm or ulceration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized invasive cancers → **surgical excision**; high-risk/recurrent facial BCC/SCC → Mohs
★ Melanoma → **wide local excision after diagnostic biopsy**; margins depend on depth
Advanced melanoma → specialist immunotherapy, selected BRAF-targeted drugs; avoid destructive treatment before diagnosis

rows.label: Complications
items: BCC: extensive local destruction, rare metastasis; SCC: nodal metastasis, especially high-risk sites/immunosuppression
Melanoma: distant metastases, including brain; immunotherapy → colitis, endocrinopathies, pneumonitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Broad-spectrum SPF ≥30**, reapply every 2 hours/outdoors after swimming; shade, protective clothing, no tanning
Self-examination, postcancer follow-up; suspicious lesions require evaluation despite uncertain population-screening benefit

rows.label: Mimics
items: Seborrheic keratosis: waxy stuck-on plaque; atypical lesions still biopsy
Dermatofibroma: firm papule with dimple sign
Benign nevus: stable symmetric uniform appearance

table.title: Nonmelanoma patterns
rows: Assess high-risk features and regional nodes
Pearly rolled edge, telangiectasia, central ulcer
Treat despite slow growth; local invasion

skin-cancer.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AAD melanoma guidance](https://www.aad.org/member/clinical-quality/guidelines/melanoma); established keratinocyte-cancer and photoprotection teaching.

spinal-cord-compression.name: Spinal cord compression
spinal-cord-compression.scope: Neoplastic spinal cord compression (epidural metastases, dexamethasone, emergent MRI), spinal epidural abscess (fever, IV drug use, empiric antibiotics), cauda equina syndrome, surgical decompression
spinal-cord-compression.core: Back pain with new weakness, sensory changes or sphincter dysfunction requires urgent MRI to identify reversible neural compression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known breast, prostate, lung, renal cancer or myeloma → epidural metastases
IV drug use, bacteremia, diabetes, spinal procedure or immunosuppression → epidural abscess
Large lumbar disc herniation, trauma or spinal stenosis → cauda equina compression

rows.label: Clues
items: Progressive nocturnal pain, pain with cough/strain, radicular symptoms; deficits may be initially subtle
Cord lesion: sensory level, spastic weakness, hyperreflexia below lesion after acute phase
★ Cauda equina: **saddle anesthesia, urinary retention**, reduced anal tone, asymmetric flaccid leg weakness
Epidural abscess: fever/back pain ± deficit; classic triad often incomplete

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Epidural tumor, infection or disc material compresses neural tissue and impairs blood supply
Longstanding compression produces irreversible ischemic injury; bladder dysfunction signals advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urgent contrast MRI** of suspected region; whole spine for suspected metastatic compression
Postvoid residual supports retention assessment but normal result does not exclude early cauda equina syndrome
Suspected abscess → blood cultures, CBC, ESR/CRP; image before LP
MRI unavailable/contraindicated → CT myelography; ordinary radiographs cannot exclude epidural pathology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Malignant compression with deficit → **dexamethasone immediately**, urgent neurosurgery/radiation consultation
Tumor → decompression/stabilization ± radiotherapy; choice depends on stability, neurologic function and prognosis
★ Epidural abscess → **vancomycin + cefepime**, cultures; urgent decompression for deficits or instability
Cauda equina syndrome → emergency spinal surgical assessment and **decompression**
Immobilize if instability suspected; bladder drainage and analgesia during definitive treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent paralysis, bowel/bladder dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, pressure injuries and VTE
Abscess → sepsis; steroids can worsen uncontrolled infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Rapid assessment of cancer-associated new back pain; sterile procedures and prompt bacteremia treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mechanical strain: normal neurologic exam, no sphincter symptoms
Transverse myelitis: intrinsic cord lesion without external compression
Peripheral neuropathy: distal symmetric findings without sensory level

spinal-cord-compression.evidence: Not checked online; established neurologic and oncologic emergency principles.

testicular-torsion.name: Testicular torsion
testicular-torsion.scope: Testicular torsion, absent cremasteric reflex, bell-clapper deformity, Doppler ultrasound, surgical detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy
testicular-torsion.core: Sudden unilateral scrotal pain with vomiting in an adolescent is spermatic cord torsion until excluded; salvage depends on immediate action.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Bell-clapper deformity permits excessive intravaginal rotation; often bilateral anatomic predisposition
Pubertal peak; may follow sleep, activity, or minor trauma; neonates can have extravaginal torsion

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **High-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex**, diffuse tenderness and swelling
Pain may present as lower abdominal discomfort without volunteered scrotal symptoms
Prior self-resolving attacks suggest intermittent torsion; symptom resolution does not eliminate recurrence risk
Delayed fever/erythema can occur; no single examination finding reliably excludes torsion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cord rotation obstructs venous drainage then arterial inflow → progressive ischemia
Viability falls rapidly with delay; greatest salvage when detorsion occurs within about 6 hours

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ High clinical suspicion → **immediate urologic exploration**, no imaging delay
Equivocal presentation → **color Doppler ultrasound**, comparing perfusion with opposite testis
Reduced/absent flow or twisted cord supports diagnosis; preserved flow possible in partial/intermittent torsion
Urinalysis for infection if uncertain; pyuria does not automatically exclude simultaneous torsion
Examine both testes in boys with unexplained acute abdominal pain; ultrasound cannot overrule compelling clinical findings

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Urgent surgical detorsion + bilateral orchiopexy**; orchiectomy only if nonviable
NPO, IV analgesia, fluids as needed; call urology while preparing operation
★ If surgical delay unavoidable → **manual outward detorsion** as bridge; direction sometimes reversed
Pain relief after manual detorsion still requires operative confirmation and fixation; residual twisting possible

rows.label: Complications
items: Infarction, testicular loss, later atrophy, reduced fertility; endocrine function often maintained by opposite testis
Reperfusion does not guarantee long-term viability; follow-up for atrophy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Contralateral fixation addresses shared anatomy; evaluate recurrent episodic scrotal pain promptly
Teach adolescents to report sudden pain immediately despite embarrassment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Epididymitis: gradual pain, urinary/STI symptoms, increased epididymal Doppler flow
Appendix testis torsion: focal superior-pole tenderness, blue-dot sign, preserved testicular flow
Incarcerated hernia: irreducible inguinoscrotal mass, possible bowel obstruction

testicular-torsion.evidence: Not checked online; established urologic emergency assessment and salvage principles.

thoracic-trauma.name: Thoracic trauma
thoracic-trauma.scope: Blunt and penetrating chest trauma, blunt cardiac injury, blunt aortic injury, diaphragmatic rupture, pulmonary contusion
thoracic-trauma.core: Chest trauma with respiratory or circulatory compromise requires immediate treatment of life-threatening injuries before definitive imaging.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-speed deceleration, steering-wheel impact, crush injuries, penetrating wounds
Lower chest wounds can cross diaphragm and injure abdominal organs

rows.label: Clues
items: Unilateral absent breath sounds, shock, distended neck veins → tension pneumothorax
Flail segment: paradoxical movement; associated lung injury drives hypoxemia
Delayed respiratory deterioration after blunt impact → pulmonary contusion
Left thoracic bowel sounds or elevated hemidiaphragm → diaphragmatic rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pleural pressure or pericardial blood impairs venous return → obstructive shock
Alveolar hemorrhage and edema impair gas exchange; rapid deceleration shears the aortic isthmus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Primary survey with **eFAST** and portable chest radiograph; unstable injuries treated clinically
★ Suspected aortic injury, stable → **CT angiography**; normal radiograph cannot exclude
Blunt cardiac injury → ECG and troponin; both normal effectively exclude significant injury
New arrhythmia or elevated troponin → telemetry; persistent shock → echocardiography

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tension pneumothorax → immediate needle/finger decompression → **chest tube**; no imaging delay
Open pneumothorax → vented seal and tube; hemothorax → tube and blood resuscitation
★ Initial tube blood >1500 mL or persistent >200 mL/h → operative exploration
Tamponade with shock/arrest → surgical drainage; pericardiocentesis only temporizing
Contusion/flail chest → oxygen, regional/multimodal analgesia, pulmonary hygiene; intubate for respiratory failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Contusion → ARDS; retained hemothorax → empyema
Rib fractures → splinting, atelectasis, pneumonia; cardiac injury → arrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seat belts, vehicle safety systems and protective equipment reduce injury risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cardiogenic shock: ventricular dysfunction without pericardial compression
Abdominal hemorrhage: free intraperitoneal fluid; may coexist with thoracic injury

thoracic-trauma.evidence: Not checked online; established ATLS-based teaching.

table.title: Definitive associated-injury management
rows: IV esmolol if tolerated; endovascular repair

thyroid-nodules-and-cancer.name: Thyroid nodules and cancer
thyroid-nodules-and-cancer.scope: Evaluation (TSH, ultrasound, FNA), benign goiter (multinodular goiter, compressive symptoms), thyroid cancer types
thyroid-nodules-and-cancer.core: A thyroid nodule requires functional assessment and ultrasound risk stratification; suspicious nonfunctioning nodules require cytologic evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Childhood head/neck irradiation, familial thyroid cancer, MEN 2
Multinodular goiter: iodine deficiency, age; multiple nodules do not exclude malignancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Hard fixed lesion, cervical nodes, rapid growth or persistent hoarseness increase cancer concern
Large benign goiter → dysphagia, positional dyspnea, tracheal compression
Anaplastic cancer: older adult with rapidly enlarging invasive neck mass

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Follicular-derived tumors differ in differentiation and spread; C-cell tumors produce calcitonin
Autonomous nodules synthesize hormone without pituitary stimulation and rarely contain malignancy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH and thyroid ultrasound** first; document cervical nodes and suspicious features
★ Low TSH → radionuclide scan; hot nodule generally **no FNA**
Normal/high TSH → ultrasound-guided FNA by sonographic risk and size
High/intermediate suspicion ≥1 cm → FNA; low suspicion ≥1.5 cm; very low suspicion ≥2 cm
★ Follicular neoplasm on FNA → diagnostic lobectomy; **capsular/vascular invasion** requires histology

rows.label: Tx
items: Benign asymptomatic nodule → ultrasound follow-up; compressive or substernal goiter → surgery
Differentiated cancer → lobectomy/thyroidectomy by risk; selected higher-risk cases → radioactive iodine
★ Medullary cancer → thyroidectomy; evaluate **pheochromocytoma before surgery**
Anaplastic disease → airway planning, multidisciplinary systemic/local treatment; radioiodine ineffective

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury → hoarseness; bilateral injury → airway obstruction
Post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism → hypocalcemia; expanding hematoma → emergency decompression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid unnecessary neck radiation; RET-positive families → counseling and preventive thyroidectomy planning

rows.label: Mimics
items: Thyroiditis: tenderness or inflammatory history, transient dysfunction
Thyroglossal cyst: midline mass moves with tongue protrusion

table.title: Cancer signatures
rows: Orphan Annie nuclei; psammoma bodies; lymphatic spread

thyroid-nodules-and-cancer.evidence: Not checked online; established ATA nodule evaluation and board-level management.

transfusion-reactions.name: Transfusion reactions
transfusion-reactions.scope: Acute hemolytic, febrile nonhemolytic, TRALI, TACO, anaphylactic, delayed hemolytic, massive transfusion complications
transfusion-reactions.core: New symptoms during transfusion require stopping the transfusion immediately and evaluating hemolysis, infection and cardiopulmonary compromise.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior transfusion/pregnancy → alloantibodies; IgA deficiency with anti-IgA → anaphylaxis
Heart/kidney failure, rapid infusion, older age → circulatory overload

rows.label: Clues
items: Delayed hemolysis: hemoglobin falls with jaundice days–weeks after apparently compatible transfusion
Bacterial contamination: high fever, rigors, profound hypotension; platelets particularly vulnerable
Isolated urticaria without systemic symptoms suggests mild allergic reaction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ABO mismatch → complement-mediated intravascular lysis; anamnestic antibodies → delayed extravascular hemolysis
TRALI: inflammatory pulmonary capillary leak; TACO: hydrostatic pressure from excess circulating volume

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Keep IV access with saline; **recheck patient/unit identity**, notify blood bank
Hemolysis workup: DAT, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, plasma/urine hemoglobin; send unit and blood samples
Fever/shock → patient and product cultures; dyspnea → chest radiograph, oxygenation, volume assessment
Suspected febrile nonhemolytic reaction remains diagnosis of exclusion after hemolysis/sepsis evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute hemolysis → IV saline, support renal perfusion, treat shock/DIC; **never restart unit**
★ Anaphylaxis → **IM epinephrine**, airway support; future washed or IgA-deficient products
TRALI → supportive oxygen/ventilation; diuretics generally unhelpful unless concomitant overload
TACO → upright positioning, oxygen, **IV furosemide**; slow future transfusions
Suspected contamination → broad IV antibiotics; mild isolated allergy → diphenhydramine after clinical reassessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute hemolysis → AKI, DIC; severe pulmonary reactions → respiratory failure
Massive transfusion → citrate hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, dilutional thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Bedside identification and crossmatch; leukoreduction reduces febrile reactions
Massive hemorrhage → balanced blood components, temperature and ionized calcium monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Underlying sepsis: symptoms may precede infusion; cultures clarify
Aspiration: event-linked infiltrate without transfusion-specific mechanism

transfusion-reactions.evidence: Not checked online; established transfusion-medicine definitions.

traumatic-brain-injury.name: Traumatic brain injury
traumatic-brain-injury.scope: Epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma, cerebral contusion, diffuse axonal injury, concussion, elevated ICP
traumatic-brain-injury.core: Head trauma ranges from transient functional disturbance to expanding hemorrhage; serial neurologic deterioration requires urgent imaging and neurosurgical assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Falls, crashes, assault, sports; anticoagulation increases bleeding
Older age, alcohol use and cerebral atrophy predispose to bridging-vein injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Headache, vomiting, amnesia; focal deficit or progressive somnolence suggests structural injury
★ **Unilateral fixed dilated pupil + declining consciousness** → uncal herniation
Cushing response: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing; late sign of critically elevated ICP

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impact/shear → secondary edema, ischemia, excitotoxicity
Rising intracranial volume → reduced cerebral perfusion; hypotension/hypoxia sharply worsen secondary injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ABCs/cervical protection → **GCS, pupils, focal examination**, repeated serially
**Noncontrast head CT** for moderate/severe injury or mild injury with high-risk features
High-risk features: anticoagulation, skull-fracture signs, focal deficit, repeated vomiting, worsening symptoms
GCS 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, ≤8 severe; diffuse axonal injury may require MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **GCS ≤8 → intubate** with spinal protection; prevent hypoxemia/hypotension; reverse anticoagulants promptly
Expanding hematoma, mass effect or deterioration → urgent neurosurgical evacuation; observation only with close monitoring
★ Elevated ICP → head elevation, analgesia/sedation, **hypertonic saline or mannitol**; treat sustained ICP >22 mm Hg
Herniation → brief hyperventilation as bridge; avoid routine prophylactic hyperventilation and corticosteroids
Severe/high-risk TBI → levetiracetam for 7 days; refractory ICP → neurosurgical decompression

rows.label: Complications
items: Posttraumatic seizures, chronic cognitive/behavioral impairment, postconcussion syndrome, hydrocephalus
Skull-base fracture → CSF leak/meningitis; avoid nasal instrumentation with suspected basilar fracture

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seatbelts, helmets, fall prevention; avoid alcohol-related injury
Concussion: no same-day sports; relative rest 24–48 hours → graded recovery/clearance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Intoxication: may coexist; exclude intracranial injury before attributing depressed consciousness to substances
Hypoglycemia: immediate glucose testing identifies reversible altered mental status

table.title: Injury patterns
rows: Temporal impact; middle meningeal artery; lucid interval
Bridging-vein rupture; gradual or acute decline
Crescent; crosses sutures, limited by dural reflections
Immediate prolonged coma after rotational acceleration
Transient headache, amnesia, cognitive slowing after impact
